units.translation: 1515a. Gorgon's freshly cut head: When Perseus was living on Seriphos with his mother at the house of Dictys and had reached manhood, Polydectes, the brother of Dictys on his mother's side, who was king of Seriphos, saw Danae and fell in love with her, but was at a loss as to how to sleep with her. So he prepared a feast and invited many others and Perseus himself. When Perseus asked on what account the banquet was being held, and he said it was for a horse, Perseus said, "For the head of the Gorgon." After the feast, on the next day, when the other guests brought their horses and Perseus too, he would not accept his, but demanded the head of the Gorgon according to the promise; and he said that if he did not bring it, he would take his mother. Perseus, grieved, went away to the farthest part of the island, lamenting his misfortune. Hermes appeared to him and questioned him, and learned the cause of his lamentation.

He leads him, telling him to take courage, first to the Graeae, daughters of Phorcys, Pemphredo and Enyo and Deino, with Athena having gone ahead. And he steals their eye and tooth as they pass them to one another; they, perceiving it, cry out and beg him to give back the eye and the tooth, for the three used them in turn, one at a time. Perseus says that he has them and will return them if they show him the Nymphs who have the cap of Hades, the winged sandals, and the kibisis. They tell him, and Perseus gives them back. And going with Hermes to the Nymphs, he asks for and receives them, binds on the winged sandals, slings the kibisis over his shoulders, and puts the cap of Hades on his head. Then he flies to the ocean and the Gorgons, with Hermes and Athena accompanying him; he finds them asleep. These gods instruct him how to cut off the head while turned away, and they point out Medusa, who alone of the Gorgons was mortal. He approaches and cuts it off, puts it in the kibisis, and flees. They, perceiving it, pursue him but do not see him. Perseus, arriving at Seriphos, goes to Polydectes and bids him assemble the people, so that he may show them the head of the Gorgon, knowing that if they saw it, they would become stones. Polydectes gathers the crowd and bids him show it. He, turning away, takes it out of the kibisis and shows it, and those who saw it became stones. Athena took the head from Perseus and placed it on her aegis; Hermes returned the kibisis, the sandals, and the cap to the Nymphs. Pherecydes relates this in the second book (3 F 11 J.).
